Health data can be organised into three main types by structure: structured, semi-structured, and unstructured data [1]. Structured data is organised into a clear format, usually rows and columns with predefined variables [1]. Examples of structured data include monthly facility reports and laboratory test registers [1].

A dataset is a collection of records, a variable is one type of information in it, and an indicator is a calculated summary measure [1]. A dataset is one row, a variable is one spreadsheet, and an indicator is one patient. A dataset and an indicator are the same, but a variable is different [1].

Internal sources are generated within your organisation, while external sources are produced by others such as national statistics offices or international agencies [1][2]. This difference is crucial in understanding the quality, methodological quality, and representation of the data [2]. Internal sources are often more detailed and frequently updated, but may have gaps and quality issues [2]. External sources, on the other hand, are usually survey-based and collected less frequently than routine data [2].

Data governance in public health refers to the organised system that guides how health data is handled from the moment it is collected to the moment it is archived. It defines who is responsible for data, who is allowed to access it, and what standards must be followed to protect it. This framework is essential in public health because it ensures that data is used ethically and legally, while creating conditions for high-quality analysis and effective collaboration. [1]

A data governance framework is essential in public health because it ensures that data is handled ethically and legally, while creating conditions for high-quality analysis and effective collaboration. It helps ensure that data is used responsibly, with strong security safeguards, and that privacy, confidentiality, and security are prioritised, especially when dealing with identifiable patient information. The key dimensions of data quality are Accuracy, Completeness, Timeliness, and Validity [1][2]. These dimensions provide a simple checklist for judging whether data are ready to be used. Data quality dimensions give a clear understanding of the degree to which a dataset can be trusted to reflect reality and support sound conclusions [1].

A typical 4-step quality assurance process for public health data starts with basic validation at the point of data entry, followed by supervisors or information officers reviewing reports, comparing them with previous periods, and following up on unusual values or missing submissions. At intervals, teams may verify figures against source documents, such as clinic registers, and correct errors where needed. Feedback to facilities closes the loop, explaining what went wrong and helping prevent the same problems in future. Some programmes also organise more formal data quality audits, where selected indicators are systematically checked across several sites to identify common weaknesses. [2]

Data wrangling is the process of transforming raw, messy data into an analysis-ready dataset. It includes all the practical work that sits between receiving a file and being able to use it to answer a question. Data wrangling helps to make the dataset consistent, complete enough for the task at hand, and reliable for decisions that affect programmes and populations. [2][2]

Line charts are the main tool for showing how an indicator changes over time. They rely on temporal data on the horizontal axis and numerical data on the vertical axis. Values at regular time points (days, weeks, months) are plotted and then connected by a line. [1][2]

When interpreting a public health time series, the key features to look for are: Level - the overall height of the series, indicating whether the indicator is at a low, moderate, or high level; Trend - the long-term direction, showing whether there is a gradual increase, decrease, or stable pattern over months or years; Seasonality - repeating patterns, such as values rising and falling in a regular cycle; and Unusual peaks or drops - deviations from the usual pattern, indicating potential outbreaks or other issues. Generalised Linear Models (GLMs) are statistical models that quantify which factors drive patterns, clarify relationships between risk factors and outcomes, and estimate how strongly different characteristics are associated with key health events [2]. They are useful in public health as they help identify who is most at risk and predict important outcomes in a transparent and interpretable way [2]. GLMs can handle different types of data, such as binary outcomes, and are the logical next step to make analysis more sophisticated [2]. By using GLMs, public health professionals can provide a foundation for machine learning and text analytics methods that follow [1].

Logistic regression is used for binary outcomes, predicting whether an event (e.g. getting sick) is likely to happen [1][3]. Poisson regression is used for count outcomes, predicting how often events (e.g. disease cases) occur over time or across places [1][3]. The main difference between the two is the type of outcome they model, with logistic regression handling binary outcomes and Poisson regression handling count outcomes [1][3].
GLMs can handle different types of data, including binary outcomes, count data, and continuous data. [2][2][3]

Machine Learning differs from traditional statistical models in public health because it learns complex patterns from data to make predictions, whereas traditional statistical models explain relationships and estimate risks using interpretable statistical models. Machine Learning algorithms can handle large or complex public health datasets, whereas traditional statistical models may struggle with such data. This difference allows Machine Learning to forecast outcomes, flag high-risk cases, and support decisions in situations where traditional models may not be effective. [2][3]

In supervised learning, features are inputs or characteristics of a case, while labels are the known outcomes or responses associated with those features. A random forest combines the predictions of its trees by taking a majority vote across the trees for categorical outcomes and calculating an average for numerical outcomes. This aggregation cancels out individual quirks and produces a more stable, reliable prediction. [1][3]

A model can look "excellent" on the data it was trained on due to overfitting, where it has memorized many details instead of identifying learning patterns [1]. To check this, analysts usually split the data into a training set and a test set, and then train and test the model on each [2]. However, even after validation, practical issues remain, such as the model's inability to generalize to new data or the need for regular review and updating to ensure its accuracy [1][2]. This is because services, reporting practices, and disease patterns evolve over time [1].

Natural Language Processing (NLP) helps computers turn unstructured text into usable data for public health by scanning text for early event signals, summarizing thousands of reports into key themes, and understanding community perceptions around interventions [1][2]. This process turns unstructured words into timely, actionable insights that strengthen surveillance, response, and risk communication. NLP applications include event detection, topic clustering, and sentiment or perception monitoring [3].
A simple NLP pipeline consists of four steps: start with raw text, break it into pieces, clean it, and then turn words into numbers. [2][3]
